name: NarrativeQA
summary: 10,557 questions about the plots of 355 books and film scripts, written from Wikipedia plot summaries by people told to imagine testing someone who had read the story, with two reference answers each.
overview:
NarrativeQA asks about stories rather than passages. The authors paired 1,572 books from Project Gutenberg and film scripts from the web with the Wikipedia plot summary of the same work, then had crowdworkers read only the summary and write questions, telling them to imagine they were setting a test for someone who had read the whole story but not the summary. Answers had to be in the worker's own words, which the interface enforced by blocking copying, so a reference answer is a short free-form phrase, averaging under five words, rather than a span to be found. A second worker checked that each question could be answered from the summary and supplied a second reference answer; only 2.3% were judged unanswerable. It was published in TACL in 2018 by DeepMind with 46,765 questions. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.07040)

The dataset defines two settings. In the summaries setting a system answers from the plot summary, around 650 tokens, which is the context the question was written from. In the full-story setting it answers from the whole book or script, averaging 58,000 tokens in this split and reaching 405,000, which the authors proposed as a test no reader of the time could handle by brute force: their models had to retrieve 200-token chunks first. The questions are the same in both settings, so the pair measures how much of an answer survives the move from a tidy summary to the entire narrative. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.07040)

Answers are scored against the two references with generation metrics rather than exact match, and even on the summaries the authors' best model fell well short of a person: a span-prediction reader reached 36.30 ROUGE-L on this test split against 57.02 for one human reference scored against the other, and an oracle that picks the best sentence of the summary reached about 59.9. On the full stories the same metrics collapsed to about 14 ROUGE-L, which is why NarrativeQA became a standard long-context benchmark and appears in later long-context suites. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.07040)
methodology:
This snapshot contains the complete official test split: 10,557 questions about 355 stories, 178 film scripts and 177 books, with both reference answers for every question and the Wikipedia plot summary of every story. The training split of 32,747 questions over 1,102 stories and the validation split of 3,461 over 115 are not imported, nor are the tokenised copies of the questions, answers, and summaries that the upstream files carry beside the originals. The pinned commit is the current head of the repository; the data files have not changed since the dataset was published, and the last commits only updated the download script's URLs. [Repository at the pinned commit](https://github.com/google-deepmind/narrativeqa/tree/904246f6d1fe99a99a08a03501fe3e619af2cee5)

Each Task Prompt is the question, two lines naming the story and its kind as upstream records them, and the plot summary. This is the summaries setting, which is also the setting the questions were written for. The full texts are not reproduced: upstream does not ship them either, shipping instead a script that downloads them from Project Gutenberg and film-script sites, and the redistribution review records why they stay out. Summaries in this split run from 201 to 990 words, averaging 570, and a story carries between 23 and 50 questions, averaging 29.7.

The Solution is the two reference answers, one per line, in the upstream order: the first from the worker who wrote the question, the second from the worker who validated it. Both count as correct, and the official metrics take the better match, so a solution shows two different wordings of the same answer rather than two different answers. Upstream records no identifier for a question, so keys combine the story's document identifier with the question's position among that story's questions in the pinned file, and prompt and solution links point at that question's line in it.

Every story's summary is credited. The upstream repository keeps the summaries in a `third_party/wikipedia` directory with the Wikipedia address of each page recorded in `documents.csv`, and the ATTRIBUTION.md the importer regenerates lists all 355 stories with those addresses. The importer uses only Python's standard library, checks that every story in the split has a summary and questions, and can be rerun with python3 data/narrativeqa/import.py.
scoring:
An answer is free text, so the dataset is scored with generation metrics against the two references: BLEU-1, BLEU-4, METEOR, and ROUGE-L, computed after lowercasing and removing final punctuation, taking the better of the two references. The authors also report mean reciprocal rank, by having a system rank the candidate answers of all questions about one story, which tests whether an answer is specific enough to belong to its own question. There is no official scoring script in the repository and no leaderboard, so published numbers come from each paper's own implementation of these metrics. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.07040)

The two settings are reported separately and are not comparable: a number computed from the plot summary measures reading a 650-token passage, while a number computed from the full story measures finding the relevant part of a novel. Later work often reports exact match and token F1 instead, which the free-form answers make harsher, and long-context suites that include NarrativeQA usually use their own prompt format, so scores across papers need care before they are compared.

Benchopedia stores the questions, the plot summaries, and both reference answers. It does not run any scorer or publish model scores for this snapshot.
limitations:
The questions were written from the summary, not from the story, by workers who had never read the story. A question can therefore turn on something the summary happens to mention, and the dataset's own full-story setting asks a system to answer from a text the question's author never saw; the authors note the summary is a condensed and interpreted account of the work. Questions about authors or actors and yes-or-no questions were excluded by instruction, so the question styles are narrower than the framing suggests. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.07040)

Two references per question is thin for free-form answers. Workers were told to use their own words and were blocked from copying, so a correct answer phrased a third way can score poorly on BLEU or ROUGE-L against both; the human figure the paper reports, 57.02 ROUGE-L, is one reference scored against the other and shows how much the metric penalises paraphrase. With no official scorer, differences between papers' metric implementations and prompt formats can be larger than the differences between systems.

The stories are a particular collection: public-domain books from Project Gutenberg, so mostly published before 1930, and film scripts scraped from fan sites, which skew towards English-language popular cinema of the late twentieth century. The summaries are 2017 Wikipedia plot sections with no revision recorded, so the article a reader finds today may describe the plot differently. Nothing in this snapshot reproduces the stories, and the addresses upstream records for them point at third-party sites that have changed since 2017.

The split has been public since 2017 and carries no canary string, and both the stories and their Wikipedia summaries are long-standing web text, so a model may have read the works, the summaries, and these questions and answers in training. There is no held-out portion that avoids this.
